0.022µF vs 0.047µF Guitar Tone Capacitors

Compare capacitance in the tone branch, with the source impedance and control settings that make the comparison meaningful.

Published 4 October 2026

In this guide
  1. Read the value correctly
  2. What increasing capacitance changes
  3. Compare at more than one tone position
  4. Conventions are useful, not compulsory
  5. What to specify when buying a part
  6. A repeatable selection process
  7. Next steps

Read the value correctly

The same capacitance in different units
MicrofaradsNanofaradsPicofarads
0.022 µF22 nF22,000 pF
0.047 µF47 nF47,000 pF

The 0.047 µF value is a little more than twice 0.022 µF. It is not a resistance and it does not state a capacitor’s physical size or construction. Unit errors are easy when reading tiny markings, so confirm the part’s code against its documentation or a suitable capacitance measurement before installation.

A nominal value is a target. Tolerance describes the allowed deviation, and an actual measurement helps make comparisons repeatable. If a circuit’s attached components interfere with measurement, isolate the capacitor rather than interpreting the reading as a definite component value.

What increasing capacitance changes

For an ideal capacitor, |Xc| = 1 / (2πfC). At the same frequency, 0.047 µF therefore has lower capacitive reactance than 0.022 µF. In the conventional tone-loading branch, that changes the impedance presented toward ground. The result depends on the tone resistance, pickup impedance and the other connected loads.

At a low tone-resistance setting, the larger value generally affects a lower part of the frequency range and can give a different rolled-down response. That is more precise than saying that one value simply removes twice as much treble. The full pickup network can have resonant behaviour; the effect is not a universal cut-off determined by the capacitor alone.

Compare at more than one tone position

At tone up, the tone resistance limits the branch’s loading, so a capacitance difference may be less prominent than at tone down. At intermediate positions, taper controls which resistance is being used. Knob markings do not guarantee the same electrical resistance across two different pots.

For a meaningful experiment, keep the same pot, pickup, volume position, cable and amplifier input. Compare the capacitors at fixed settings, including the setting you actually use. If the pot or cable is changed at the same time, you have changed more than one variable and cannot confidently assign the result to capacitance.

Conventions are useful, not compulsory

0.022 µF is often associated with humbucker circuits and 0.047 µF with single-coil circuits. Both values also appear outside those conventions. Pickup inductance, desired adjustment range and the original circuit design are better reasons for a choice than the pickup family name on its own.

A player who rarely rolls tone down may care more about the available intermediate range. Another player may want a particular fully rolled-down response. Neither preference makes one capacitor universally correct. Begin with the existing specification if repairing a working instrument, and change deliberately if experimenting.

What to specify when buying a part

Choose the required capacitance, an appropriate tolerance and voltage rating, sensible lead spacing and dimensions that fit the cavity. Reliability, insulation and repeatable assembly are practical benefits. They do not require a claim that a particular dielectric or historic casing adds an otherwise unexplained sound.

Equivalent values need evidence for unequal claims

A premium component can offer useful construction or QC. Do not infer audible superiority from its material name, colour or price alone. Identify a measurable difference before assigning it an electrical explanation.

Make sure capacitor leads cannot short to the casing or neighbouring terminals. A good component with poor installation can produce a fault that overwhelms the subtle comparison you intended to make.

A repeatable selection process

Write down the current component value and the symptom or change you want. Check that the tone branch is wired correctly first. Compare candidate values with the same assumptions in Signal Forge, then use the physical wiring reference to verify the connection. Respect the tool’s supported-model limits rather than treating a simulated curve as a complete listening test.

Keep a note of the measured capacitance and the settings used in the comparison. If neither value gives the useful control range you want, consider the tone taper and surrounding loading before accumulating more parts. This makes the choice a controlled circuit decision instead of a search for a mythical capacitor.
